d: The resting follicle: a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I inside one layer of flat granulosa cells. The whole lifetime supply forms before birth and shrinks by atresia.
The vascular layer of cells outside a follicle's basement membrane. Under LH, it turns cholesterol into androstenedione, the androgen that granulosa cells convert to estradiol.
The avascular cells lining the follicle inside its basement membrane. FSH induces their aromatase, which converts theca androgens to estradiol. They also secrete inhibin B and AMH.
The mid-cycle burst of LH released when sustained high estradiol switches the pituitary to positive feedback. It restarts meiosis I and triggers ovulation about 36 hours after it begins.
The luteinized granulosa and theca cells left after ovulation. It secretes progesterone for about 14 days, then becomes a corpus albicans unless hCG from an embryo rescues it.
The superficial endometrial layer, fed by spiral arteries, that thickens each cycle and is shed at menses. It regrows from the stratum basalis, which is fed by straight arteries.

The change of granulosa and theca cells into progesterone-secreting luteal cells after the LH surge. They fill with lipid, capillaries invade the granulosa layer, and the follicle becomes the corpus luteum.
The progesterone-driven change of endometrial stromal cells into large, glycogen-rich decidual cells. It begins in the late secretory phase and continues in pregnancy.
The cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, driven by LH in theca cells. It turns cholesterol into pregnenolone, the first and rate-limiting step of all steroid hormone synthesis.
